chunks: From him, from Safwan and Fadalah, from al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): A man manumits his slave conditionally (mudabbir), then later needs the money (to buy him back or use the value). He said: 'If he needs the money, it is for him; he may sell (the slave) if he wishes, or he may free (him) completely, and that is from the third (part of the value/ownership).'.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: What these narrations include regarding the permissibility of selling the mudabbir is actually the permissibility of selling his service/labor, not the neck (full ownership), because we have clarified that as long as he is mudabbir, the owner possesses only his service for the duration of his life. And if he does not possess anything else from him, then selling anything other than that is not valid from him. And we will also cite later what confirms this.

As for what the preceding narrations included regarding that conditional manumption is like a will, and a person may retract his will, the meaning in it is that the owner may annul the conditional manumption, just as he may annul the will. So whenever he annuls it, the mudabbir returns to being a pure slave, at which point it is permissible for him to sell his neck (full ownership), just as it is permissible for him to sell the others among his slaves. And whenever he does not annul the conditional manumption and wishes to sell him, it is not permissible for him to sell except the service, according to what we have presented.
And that which adds clarification to this is what he narrated:

key_terms.خِدْمَة: Service or labor of the slave
key_terms.رَقَبَة: The neck, referring to full ownership of the slave
key_terms.مُدَبَّر: A slave who has been conditionally manumitted

ai.seo_question: What are the rights of an owner regarding a conditionally manumitted slave (mudabbir) in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the juristic distinction between selling the 'neck' (full ownership) versus the 'service' of a *mudabbir*, a status treated as a revocable will (*wasiyya*) where the owner retains control until the condition is met. Scholars like Muhammad ibn al-Hasan explain that if the owner annuls the manumption, the slave reverts to pure servitude, allowing for the sale of the neck; otherwise, only the service is alienable. This highlights the Shia legal principle that conditional manumption does not immediately transfer full property rights to the slave, preserving the owner's discretion.
